item.title: Free drug and protein binding
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
Most antibacterial targets are written for free (unbound) drug. Many PK models, though, are fitted to total plasma concentrations. Mixing the two is one of the most common silent errors in PTA work.

NoteScope

Modeling hygiene for exposure–effect alignment — not a dosing calculator.

What “free” means in a target

If a paper says 100% fT>MIC, the f is doing real work:

  • only unbound molecules are assumed available to interact with the pathogen (in the usual plasma-centric framing),
  • the MIC assay is typically interpreted on an unbound-equivalent scale,
  • so the simulator must compare free concentration–time to MIC.

If your model outputs total concentration and you apply a free-drug target without correction, you inflate exposure.

A minimal correction

With unbound fraction :

[ C_{}(t) = f_u C_{}(t) ]

when binding is approximately linear and constant. That assumption is often good enough for a first model — and often wrong enough to deserve a sensitivity sweep.

Where modelers get hurt

  1. Target says free; curve is total → optimistic PTA.
  2. fu taken from healthy volunteers applied to hypoalbuminemic ICU patients without comment.
  3. Site of infection ≠ plasma — epithelial lining fluid, CSF, or tissue targets need their own framing.
  4. Highly bound drugs — small fu errors become large free-exposure errors.

Practical checklist

  • Write the unit next to every plotted series: mg/L free or mg/L total.
  • Cite the fu source and whether it is fixed, covariate-dependent, or sampled.
  • Re-run PTA at lower/higher fu as a one-way sensitivity analysis.
  • For combinations, bind each component separately.

Takeaway

Align the binding state of the PK output with the binding state of the PD target. Everything else in the Monte Carlo stack inherits that decision.

item.title: Intermittent vs continuous infusion for β-lactams
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
For many β-lactams, the dominant index is fT>MIC. That makes how you deliver the daily dose a first-class modeling choice: short intermittent infusions create peaks and troughs; continuous infusion flattens the profile toward a steady free concentration.

NoteScope

PK/PD geometry of infusion mode for simulation. Not a recommendation to change bedside practice.

Same daily dose, different shape

Hold clearance, volume, fu, and MIC fixed. Change only the input rate:

  • Intermittent: repeated short infusions → oscillating .
  • Extended infusion: longer infusions per dose → higher troughs, softer peaks.
  • Continuous: constant rate → approach to steady state .

For a pure fT>MIC rule, continuous infusion often converts the question to whether stays above a multiple of MIC for the entire interval.

What your simulator must not forget

  1. Loading dose — continuous regimens often need an initial bolus; omitting it underestimates early fT>MIC.
  2. Stability / administration constraints — model scenario ≠ pharmacy reality; label assumptions.
  3. Renal function — Css moves with clearance; eGFR strata can dominate PTA differences more than infusion cosmetics.
  4. Targets as ratios — some β-lactam analyses use (or similar) rather than raw T>MIC percent.

Modeling comparison template

When you compare intermittent vs continuous:

  • freeze the virtual population and MIC grid,
  • change only the dosing input,
  • report PTA curves on the same MIC axis,
  • show early-interval behavior separately if loading doses differ.

Takeaway

Infusion mode is not a plotting preference. It changes the exposure geometry that fT>MIC (and Css/MIC) rules evaluate.

item.title: Joint targets for β-lactam / β-lactamase inhibitor pairs
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
A β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (BL/BLI) pair is not one drug with two names. One component usually provides antibacterial exposure; the other protects that exposure from enzymes. Adequacy is therefore often a joint event.

NoteScope

Simulation logic for combination PK/PD. Example framing inspired by ceftazidime–avibactam-style problems; not product-specific clinical advice.

Two clocks, one decision

Suppose:

  • Drug A (β-lactam) must satisfy a free-exposure target vs MIC,
  • Drug B (inhibitor) must stay above a threshold that preserves A’s activity.

Patient-level success is:

[ {A } {B } ]

not the average of the two success indicators.

Common modeling mistakes

  1. Collapse to one analyte — simulating only the β-lactam because “that is the antibiotic.”
  2. Report mean(PTA_A, PTA_B) as if it were joint attainment.
  3. Ignore correlation — clearances of A and B may covary; independent draws can misstate joint tails.
  4. Borrow incompatible thresholds — inhibitor targets from a different matrix, population, or regimen without labeling.

A clean joint workflow

  1. Simulate both concentration–time profiles in each virtual subject.
  2. Apply component-specific free targets.
  3. Mark joint success only when both pass.
  4. Build PTA vs MIC (or vs scenario grid) from the joint indicator.
  5. Optionally weight by MIC ecology → joint CFR.

This is the same philosophy used in provenance-aware CAZ-AVI style evidence-composite work: components stay separate until a joint rule is applied deliberately.

Takeaway

For BL/BLI pairs, protection failure is regimen failure even when the β-lactam curve looks beautiful alone. Joint PTA is an intersection, not an average.

item.title: Uncertainty and provenance in PK/PD evidence
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
A polished PTA curve can hide a messy evidence trail. The scientific question is not only “what is the probability?” but which assumptions, from which sources, under which scenario compatibility rules, produced that probability?

NoteScope

Evidence hygiene for reusable antimicrobial PK/PD simulation. Aligns with component-level evidence-composite thinking.

Provenance beats vibes

Every simulation input deserves a label:

Label idea Meaning
Directly reported Taken as published for this use
Transformed Unit change, free/total conversion, algebraic rearrange
Inherited / donor Borrowed from a related but non-identical source
Assumed / user-specified Filled to run the model; must stay visible
Scenario-generated Arises from the simulation design itself

Missingness should remain missing until a compatible donor is justified — not silently median-imputed in a methods paragraph nobody reads.

Uncertainty is layered

  1. Parameter uncertainty — IIV, residual error, covariate model.
  2. Structural uncertainty — one- vs two-compartment; infusion constraints.
  3. Evidence uncertainty — wrong population, wrong matrix, stale MIC ecology.
  4. Decision-rule uncertainty — which target threshold is “the” target?

Monte Carlo on layer 1 alone can look precise while layer 3 dominates the truth.

A minimum reporting set

  • Source list for CL, V, fu, targets, MIC weights
  • Transformation notes (free/total, units)
  • Population / scenario compatibility statement
  • Seeds, , and convergence check
  • One-way or global sensitivity on the fragile inputs

Takeaway

Reproducible PK/PD is less about prettier sampling and more about refusing to launder uncertain evidence into false certainty.

item.title: Horizontal gene transfer and MIC ecology
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is how resistance genes move sideways — across lineages and sometimes across species — often on plasmids, transposons, or integrative elements. For PK/PD, HGT matters because it can rewire the MIC distribution faster than a cloned chromosomal mutation typically would.

NoteScope

Genetics as annotation on the MIC layer used by PTA/CFR — not a full HGT mechanisms course.

From gene traffic to simulation priors

CFR needs . That probability mass is an ecological claim:

  • which species / complex,
  • which region and year,
  • which specimen mix,
  • which mechanisms dominate locally.

If a plasmid carrying a carbapenemase expands in your catchment, last year’s MIC weights can become a precise answer to an obsolete question.

Modeler habits that survive contact with HGT

  1. Date-stamp MIC sources in every CFR table.
  2. Separate mechanism strata when possible (enzyme class vs target mutation).
  3. Recompute CFR under alternative local distributions as sensitivity analysis.
  4. Do not over-interpret a single-hospital antibiogram as a universal prior.
  5. Link back to chromosome vs plasmid resistance when labeling stability vs mobility.

Takeaway

HGT does not replace pharmacometrics. It tells you when your epidemiology prior — the MIC weights under CFR — must be treated as perishable.

item.title: PK/PD targets and the MIC: what the indices actually mean
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
Antibiotic PK/PD modeling starts with one awkward fact: bacteria do not “see” the dose. They see concentration over time at the effect site, relative to a susceptibility threshold — usually the MIC.

This lesson is for modelers and microbiologists who want the indices to stop feeling like slogans.

NoteScope

Educational modeling intuition — not a dosing guide and not a substitute for clinical guidelines.

The MIC is a threshold, not a full phenotype

The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) is the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth under a defined assay. It is useful because it compresses susceptibility into a number we can put next to an exposure curve.

It is also incomplete:

  • Assay conditions can move the measured floor.
  • Tolerance and persistence can leave survivors even when the MIC looks favorable.
  • Protein binding means free (unbound) exposure often matters more than total concentration.

For simulation, treat MIC as a scenario input with uncertainty, not as biological truth.

Three classic indices

Most antibacterial PK/PD targets fall into one of three families:

Index Rough idea Typical drug classes
fT>MIC Fraction of the dosing interval that free concentration stays above MIC Many β-lactams
fAUC/MIC Integrated free exposure scaled by MIC Fluoroquinolones, vancomycin (often)
fCmax/MIC Peak free concentration relative to MIC Some concentration-dependent agents

The leading f means unbound fraction. If you simulate total concentrations but apply a free-drug target, you are mixing units.

How to choose an index in a model

Ask three questions before coding a target:

  1. Is killing time-dependent or concentration-dependent for this class in the literature you trust?
  2. Are you modeling free or total drug? Align the PK output with the PD target.
  3. Is the target joint? Combinations (for example β-lactam + inhibitor) may need two simultaneous conditions.

If the literature reports a target as “100% fT>MIC” or “fAUC/MIC ≥ 125,” that is a decision rule for simulation, not proof that every patient at that threshold is cured.

Takeaway for modelers

  • Put units and binding next to every target.
  • Sample MIC from a distribution when you care about population performance.
  • Keep the index choice traceable to a cited source, the same way you would cite a clearance equation.

item.title: PTA, CFR, and virtual populations
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
Once you have an exposure index and an MIC, the next modeling question is not “does this patient hit the target?” It is: in a population with realistic variability, how often does the regimen succeed?

That is where virtual populations, PTA, and CFR enter.

NoteScope

Methodological intuition for simulation workflows — not a clinical decision tool.

Virtual populations are controlled randomness

A virtual population is a set of simulated individuals whose PK parameters (clearance, volume, covariates such as renal function) are drawn from distributions that reflect interindividual variability.

Good practice:

  • Sample from published IIV / residual error when available.
  • Keep covariate structure explicit (for example eGFR classes).
  • Record seeds, sample size, and whether parameters are correlated.

Bad practice:

  • Drawing “nice looking” normals with no provenance.
  • Pooling incompatible populations (healthy volunteer PK used silently as ICU truth).

PTA: probability of target attainment

PTA answers: for a fixed MIC (or a fixed MIC grid), what fraction of virtual subjects meet the PK/PD target?

Example framing:

At MIC = 4 mg/L, what percentage of simulated ICU adults achieve 100% fT>MIC on regimen X?

Plot PTA against MIC to see where the regimen cliff starts.

CFR: weighting PTA by the real MIC ecology

CFR (cumulative fraction of response) folds PTA over an MIC distribution from surveillance or local epidemiology:

[ = _i (_i) P(_i) ]

PTA asks “what if MIC is X?”
CFR asks “given the MICs we actually see, how often do we succeed?”

If your MIC weights come from a different region, year, or species complex than your clinical question, CFR becomes a precise answer to the wrong question.

A minimal workflow

  1. Define regimen and PK model (with provenance).
  2. Define free-drug target(s).
  3. Simulate virtual subjects.
  4. Compute PTA on an MIC grid.
  5. Optionally weight by an MIC distribution → CFR.
  6. Report sensitivity to binding, IIV, and MIC source.

Takeaway for modelers

  • PTA is a curve over MIC; CFR is a scalar under an epidemiology prior.
  • Sample size and seed reporting are part of reproducibility, not decoration.
  • Joint targets (two drugs, two conditions) need joint PTA — not the average of two separate success rates.

item.title: Resistance, tolerance, and persistence in PK/PD language
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
In clinical conversation, “the antibiotic did not work” is often collapsed into resistance. For modeling, that collapse is expensive: it points the simulator at the wrong mechanism.

This lesson maps three survival ideas onto what a PK/PD model can and cannot see.

NoteScope

Conceptual distinctions for simulation and evidence interpretation. Related preprint context: comparative modeling of resistance, tolerance, and persistence.

Three words, three model objects

Concept Core idea What usually moves in a model
Resistance Heritable reduced susceptibility Higher MIC / shifted PD curve
Tolerance Population survives longer under drug stress without a large MIC shift Slower kill rate, longer time-kill shoulder
Persistence Small subpopulation survives much longer Biphasic kill; a refractory fraction

Resistance changes the threshold.
Tolerance and persistence change the time course of killing even when the threshold looks acceptable.

Why MIC-only PTA can look “fine” and still fail

A regimen can show high PTA against the measured MIC distribution while:

  • a tolerant population dies too slowly for the treatment duration,
  • a persistent fraction seeds relapse,
  • or the assay MIC understates the relevant effect-site challenge.

That does not make PTA useless. It means PTA answers a specific question (exposure vs threshold), not the entire clinical narrative.

Practical modeling checklist

  1. Label whether your PD endpoint is inhibition (MIC-style) or killing (time-kill / CFU decline).
  2. If you only have MIC targets, say so explicitly in the limitations.
  3. When comparing pathogens, do not assume the same survival mode — M. tuberculosis and S. aureus are a useful contrast case in the preprint above.
  4. Keep genetics in a separate layer: a plasmid-borne β-lactamase may raise MIC; a persistence program may not.

Takeaway for modelers

  • Resistance → move the MIC / PD curve.
  • Tolerance / persistence → reshape kill kinetics and duration logic.
  • Report which of the three your simulation is actually testing.

item.title: Chromosome vs plasmid resistance for PK/PD modelers
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
PK/PD models rarely simulate DNA. They simulate exposure and a phenotype — often an MIC or a kill curve. Genetics still matters, because it tells you how stable that phenotype is and how it might spread between patients or species.

This secondary-track lesson is a bridge: enough bacterial genetics to stop treating every MIC as the same kind of object.

NoteScope

Genetics-for-modelers, not a full genomics course. Pair with the PK/PD track starting at targets and MIC.

Two genomic homes for resistance

Feature Chromosomal Plasmid-borne (typical)
Inheritance Vertical (mother → daughter) Vertical and often horizontal
Dose effect Usually one/few copies per genome Copy number can amplify expression
Mobility Mostly within lineage Can jump lineages / species
Modeling implication Phenotype more lineage-stable MIC ecology can shift faster; local epidemiology ages quicker

A chromosomal target-site mutation and a plasmid β-lactamase can produce the “same” higher MIC in a table — and very different public-health and uncertainty stories.

What changes inside a PK/PD workflow

  1. MIC distribution provenance
    If resistance is plasmid-driven and locally epidemic, last year’s surveillance weights may be stale.

  2. Heterogeneity inside “one MIC”
    Same categorical MIC breakpoint can hide different enzyme burdens or copy numbers.

  3. Combination regimens
    Inhibitor partners (for example avibactam) are meaningful when the mechanism is enzyme-mediated; they are the wrong lever for some chromosomal target mutations.

  4. Uncertainty labeling
    Mark whether MIC inputs reflect a stable clonal background or a mobile element–shaped ecology.

Takeaway for modelers

  • Do not ask genetics to replace PK/PD; ask it to annotate the MIC layer.
  • Plasmid ecology → refresh surveillance weights and mechanism assumptions more aggressively.
  • Chromosomal lineage structure → stability helps, but still verify assay and species ID.
